headline: Rising long-term bond yields globally signal fiscal stress and inflation concern, generally negative for currencies unlike short-term rate rises
reasoning: Dooley explains that rising long-term bond yields are being driven by fiscal deficit concerns, large post-Covid government spending programs, and doubts about central bank resolve to contain inflation. He distinguishes between short-term and long-term rate moves: short-term rate rises are typically currency-supportive via yield differentials, while long-term yield rises are a sign of stress and tend to weaken the currency. The UK is cited as the clearest recent illustration, where a jump in long-term yields accompanied a sharp fall in the British pound.
quote: So short term interest rates going up will normally be supportive of a currency. We're in the long term uh bond yields are going up. Then often that's a sign of stress and concern around a economy. And that's often when you see a big selloff in the currency. And that's probably been most clearly illustrated by some of the concerns we've seen in the U.K. over the last 5 or 6 years. A big jump in long term bond yields has saying a sharp move lower in the British pound. So it's a different story to what we see sometimes when the short term interest rates go higher, when the long term interest rates go higher, it's generally not supportive of a currency. It's normalised, normally a sign of stress in that particular economy, that particular jurisdiction.

headline: Australian dollar remains in an established 68-72 cent trading range; next catalyst needed to break either direction

He argues the market is waiting for a new information catalyst to break the range, and sees no imminent structural move until that catalyst emerges.

This has caused markets to worry about inflation running out of control, which is pressuring the yen lower even as yields rise.

headline: Shier Lee Lim explains post-Fed USD weakness as inflation risk premium repricing rather than a dovish pivot
reasoning: The USD move was not about the Fed's decision to hold rates but about how markets read the press conference. What got priced was inflation risk premium rather than a dovish turn, with the market treating the path back to target as less defined than the statement implied. This expressed itself in the curve rather than the front end alone, with a 50 basis point twist and the largest single-day curve move in a decade. The long end rose to its highest level since 2007, break-evens moved 4-7 basis points higher, and rising break-evens alongside falling real yields is a historically unfriendly combination for the US dollar. Lim distinguishes this from an established repricing which would take the short end and dollar down together.
quote: The move wasn't really about a decision, so it was about how the market read the press conference and what it did about it. What got priced was inflation risk premium rather than a dovish turn. The market came away treating the path back to target as less defined than the statement implied. And it expressed that in the curve rather than in the front end alone... Established repricing takes the short end down and the dollar with it. And the risk premium repricing takes a long and up and does more damage. So the curve is where you could see it 50 basis points from end to end twist depending on the day. The largest single day curve move on a fat day in a decade. Front end lower long end up to its highest level since 2007.

headline: Shier Lee Lim warns rising US 30-year yields and widening break-evens set a higher global discount rate floor with spillover risk to UK and Japan
reasoning: The US 30-year yield at 5.27%, its highest since 2007, acts as the world's discount rate and is imported globally including into Australia. Widening break-evens driven by higher energy prices compound this. Lim flags that markets where the long end and currency trade off the same fiscal story — specifically the UK and Japan — are where spillover would show up first if higher US term premium pulls global long-end yields up. She notes this is a risk flag rather than a base case. She also observes that gold fell about 1.5% on Friday as real yields rose, which argues against this being a pure debasement episode, and distinguishes benign dollar weakness (rest of world catching up) from the more damaging variant.
quote: The US 30 year as you said Nadine is around 5.27 the highest since 2007. And break evens widened again on Friday as energy pushed higher. So that sets the floor under the term premium globally and prices risk assets. And if this is the cause of long dated borrowing everywhere, Australia included. So where are watch for spillover? Is that the markets where the long end and the currency trade off the same fiscal story. The UK and Japan are the obvious two. So if higher US term premium starts pulling the long end used up more broadly, that's where it shows up first. So I flagged that as a risk rather than the base case. And here's the useful track because it cuts against the alarmist version of the story. Gold actually fell about 1.5% on Friday as real yields rose. So if this were really a debasement episode goes the first place you see it, and right now you don't.

The damaging version is a true debasement episode, which would show up in gold prices first — and gold actually fell on Friday, suggesting this is not yet a debasement scenario.
